description: Our team consists of a Biomedical Engineering student, an Industrial Design Engineering student, two Telecommunications Engineering students, and an App Development student. We're five innovation enthusiasts who love taking on new challenges.
summary:
BloodTrack aims to address the difficulty of continuously monitoring the physiological
changes astronauts experience due to microgravity, especially those related to fluid
redistribution and microcirculation. To this end, it proposes developing a platform capable of
collecting, storing and analysing measurements obtained from sensors placed on different
parts of the body, creating a personalised record with graphs and comparisons that makes it
possible to track each astronaut?s progress and provide supplementary information to the
medical team. We use the AMT LAZMA-1 as the initial reference device for the FluidShift
Monitor, although the final sensor will need to be suitable for the conditions of the space
environment.
details:
BloodTrack continuously monitors how microgravity redistributes fluid in an astronaut’s body. Sensors on the neck, both arms and both legs record skin temperature and microcirculation, using the AMT LAZMA-1 as the reference Fluid Shift Monitor until a flight-qualified sensor replaces it. The platform stores those readings as a personal record and turns them into a picture the medical team can follow over time. It does not diagnose.

For any UTC day, the console shows the latest temperature and the latest perfusion-unit reading at each site, whether that sample was taken during movement, and whether the value is fine, caution or danger. A body figure carries the same colours, so a hot or poorly perfused region is visible at a glance. Because movement can imitate a real physiological change, BloodTrack also counts how many samples were movement-marked and plots those counts by hour. Empty hours are missing data, not stillness.

Over a chosen UTC range it draws the course of temperature and microcirculation for the neck, the arms and the legs, against reference bands. Daily summaries then reduce each region to how many samples were collected, the average temperature, the average flow and how often movement was registered. Together these views let the team see the day’s state, trust or discount a reading, and compare an astronaut’s progress from one day to the next.
